issue_context.title: High CPU Utilization in kube-apiserver when a large number of CRDs are created
issue_context.body:
### What happened? In [Crossplane](https://crossplane.io/), we would like to register thousands of CRDs in a single cluster representing the many Cloud services possibly from multiple Cloud Providers. In our early trials with kind clusters, we have observed that simultaneously posting just over 700 CRDs results in a CPU-utilization spike in kube-apiserver, due to the background OpenAPI spec publishing job. We were also made aware of the memory consumption [issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/101755) during CRD creation. We made similar observations in a GKE cluster on which we installed over 650 CRDs, making the total 685. Unfortunately, we could not identify the root cause but we have observed the cluster flipping between the "repairing" state and the "available" state for an extended period of time. Our observation is that the cluster could come out of the repairing state but for a couple of times, it was in repairing state again, with no new CRD registrations or object creations from our side. The only probes we utilized during this period were `kubectl get` commands. In [our tests](https://github.com/crossplane-contrib/terrajet/issues/47#issuecomment-920316141), we have observed that on an arm64 machine with 8 CPU cores, API server enters a high CPU utilization period of about 20 min after 750+ CRDs are created. If the API server saturates the CPU resources allocated to it, this may also disrupt its services. So we have a couple of questions: 1. Can we expect the fix for the memory issue referenced above improve the situation with the CPU? 2. Are there any plans for introducing the number of CRDs in a cluster as a scalability dimension in the [thresholds document](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md)? If so, is it reasonable to expect our use cases covered? 3. Is it possible/reasonable to turn off the `/openapi/v2` endpoint to prevent aggregation of the OpenAPI schemas of the CRDs? Who are the clients of this endpoint? 4. In the GKE case, is there a way to monitor kube-apiserver CPU/memory consumption, crashes, etc.? So that we can reason about our empirical observations described above. ### What did you expect to happen? We were not expecting to observe CPU usage spikes for extended periods in our tests. For the GKE cluster experiment, we were not expecting service disruptions. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Simultaneously create a large number (>650) of CRDs with OpenAPI schemas. ### Anything else we need to know? It looks like the average schema size in bytes per CRD could be a relevant parameter. If needed, we can supply those numbers assuming schemas are serialized in JSON. If you'd like to see some example CRDs we used in the above observations, please take a look at this [branch](https://github.com/ulucinar/provider-tf-azure/tree/fix-ps-670/package/crds) of one of the Crossplane providers. ### Kubernetes version
v1.21.0 in local tests where we observed high CPU utilization.
v1.20.10-gke.301 for GKE:
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"21", GitVersion:"v1.21.1", GitCommit:"5e58841cce77d4bc13713ad2b91fa0d961e69192", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-05-12T14:11:29Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/arm64"} Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"20+", GitVersion:"v1.20.10-gke.301", GitCommit:"17ad7bd6afa01033d7bd3f02ce5de56f940a915d", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-08-24T05:18:54Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.15b5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} ```
### Cloud provider
GKE
### OS version
```console # On Linux: $ cat /etc/os-release # paste output here $ uname -a # paste output here # On Windows: C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture # paste output here ```

comments:
> The only probes we utilized during this period were kubectl get commands.

We observed the API server was unresponsive during this time too, right? Was the API server timing out? (We're presuming the process OOMed and restarted somewhere else with more memory but I don't think it's possible to know for sure.)

Reading through https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/pull/251, I suspect it will fix this issue.

If I'm following correctly, each time a CRD is added or updated its [the OpenAPI controller will](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/00aab63/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/controller/openapi/controller.go#L156):

1. Build a swagger spec specifically for the defined CR, which is I think what is used for validation etc.
1. [Merge](https://github.com/kubernetes/apiextensions-apiserver/blob/ebfb0f7/pkg/controller/openapi/builder/merge.go#L24) swagger specs of all known CRDs together into one big spec.
1. [Serialise](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/blob/a3aade/pkg/handler/handler.go#L104) the giant merged spec into JSON, so it can be served by the /openapi/v2 handler.

So I imagine what's happening is that when we install 600+ CRDs the API server is crunching through that process 600 times in a row, with increasingly more CRDs in the system. It seems like everyone's profiling points to the serialisation being the main culprit so I imagine making that lazy will be the biggest win. I wonder whether there could be further wins by not having the openapi controller keep a map of all CRD schemas all the time, and merge the schemas together on every reconcile.

> In the GKE case, is there a way to monitor kube-apiserver CPU/memory consumption, crashes, etc.? So that we can reason about our empirical observations described above.

@ulucinar It does seem like there are a few insights into this from the API server's Prometheus instrumentation - namely `process_start_time_seconds`, `process_resident_memory_bytes`, and `process_cpu_seconds_total` - that are present even when the API server doesn't otherwise expose metrics we can get at (e.g. pod or container metrics).

> We made similar observations in a GKE cluster

It's worth noting that we saw the GKE cluster become unreachable during this time, but we now believe this is because we're using a zonal cluster with a single API server process that disappeared for a bit to resize to accommodate its increased compute needs.

> It's worth noting that we saw the GKE cluster become unreachable during this time, but we now believe this is because we're using a zonal cluster with a single API server process that disappeared for a bit to resize to accommodate its increased compute needs.

Hrm I'm now questioning this. Despite yesterday managing to get to ~1,200 CRDs on a regional cluster without issue today I've been unable to get above ~700 or so before the cluster becomes unresponsive - in some cases while repairing and others not. EKS seems to handle this fine, so I'm guessing it's a function of how many resources each service gives their control planes.

> Are there any plans for introducing the number of CRDs in a cluster as a scalability dimension in the thresholds document? If so, is it reasonable to expect our use cases covered?

Yeah - we should certainly do that - just didn't get to it yet...

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105932#issuecomment-953383812:

IIRC:
- each time a CRD is added or updated, apiextensions-apiserver serializes a merged spec of all CRDs 
- [every second](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c9ddd248b6d58c4c973d507be07261b96ef0cfbc/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/controllers/openapi/controller.go#L34), the aggregation layer reads the apiextensions-apiserver spec, and serializes a merged spec of all APIs if the apiextensions-apiserver spec's ETag changed.

With lazy marshalling:
- every second, apiextensions-apiserver does the serialization if a CRD was added or updated
- when a client (e.g. kubectl) queries kube-apiserver /openapi/v2 spec, the aggregation layer does the serialization if the apiextensions-apiserver spec's ETag changed

Some potential improvements we can do:
- the aggregation layer should download apiextension-apiserver openapi spec using proto instead of json
- make how often the aggregation layer polls apiextension-apiserver configurable?

> not having the openapi controller keep a map of all CRD schemas all the time, and merge the schemas together on every reconcile

I think it helps but merging the spec doesn't play as a big part in the latency as the json (de)serialization. There were some scalability data we collected when CRD went GA (not sure if they still hold): https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1015#discussion_r305521857

Our initial tests show that https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/pull/251 is likely to fix (or greatly alleviate) this issue. See https://github.com/crossplane/crossplane/issues/2649#issuecomment-956914007 for details.

Just to recap, I think we've all pinpointed serialization to be the main culprit of the high resource usage. This issue is magnified when applying 100s of CRDs in a short time period since we'll be repeating the serialization process [per CRD create](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/controller/openapi/controller.go#L194). https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/pull/251 reduces the frequency of serialization by doing it "lazily" only when a get request is received on the OpenAPI spec. 

The underlying issue is that serialization of a giant aggregated OpenAPI spec takes a lot of resources. [OpenAPI v3](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/2896-openapi-v3/README.md) aims to solve this issue by not publishing the aggregated spec and only publishing specs per group/version but it'll be a while before that becomes GA. In the short term, reducing the frequency of the serializations via https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/pull/251 looks to provide good results (seen in https://github.com/crossplane/crossplane/issues/2649#issuecomment-956914007) and is something we should look to merge/cherrypick

Also @Jefftree pointed out that we [build proto from json](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-openapi/blob/ec1f4c89925aaed16de489e6daa816bed3bd2811/pkg/handler/handler.go#L105-L112) today. We probably should look into building proto from Go structure directly. With lazy marshaling, that would help us eliminate the json serialization completely (assuming everyone uses proto)

> We probably should look into building proto from Go structure directly. With lazy marshaling, that would help us eliminate the json serialization completely (assuming everyone uses proto)

be careful about type mismatches that got covered up by serialization round tripping (int vs int64, empty list vs nil, etc) that would make deepequal checks fail

review_comments:
It's pretty twisty that Get() mutates *cache, and that calls to Get() from getSwaggerBytes() and getSwaggerPbBytes() are only protected by a read-lock.

It's not clear from the outside that cache#Get() and cache#New() are unsafe to call concurrently... and the calls to Get and New only happen to be safe because they're guarded by locks (which were primarily intended to protect reads/writes to the fields in OpenAPIService).

Not blocking for this PR, but probably worth a follow-up in kube-openapi master to clarify/clean that up
Good catch! Let's fix that up.
